summary:
Lunar Horizon is a web app for comparing lunar landing sites and dates. It combines NASA JPL Horizons positions with LRO LOLA terrain data to show when the Sun and Earth are visible from a chosen site.

Users can explore the terrain in 3D, move through time, and check a mission against their own requirements. Failed requirements link to their time intervals and a 3D view. Mission Rescue searches supported sites and dates for alternatives that meet the same requirements.

In our hypothetical example, a four-day delay increases the longest Earth-contact gap from 22 to 118 hours within the mission, exceeding a 96-hour limit. The gap reaches the mission boundary and may continue afterward. Malapert Massif meets the unchanged requirements on the delayed date for the same 14-day mission.

A guided tour introduces the workflow using NASA-derived data. Plan comparison and downloadable Mission Reports preserve the evidence for review. Rover, an optional read-only AI assistant, explains computed results and helps users navigate those views. Requirements remain UNKNOWN when the available evidence cannot decide.

We built Lunar Horizon for early mission planning and education, with the model's limits clearly stated.
details:
What we built and why it matters

Lunar Horizon helps users compare lunar landing sites and dates against a mission’s lighting and direct-to-Earth visibility requirements. We built it for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge.

At the lunar south pole, nearby terrain can hide the Sun or Earth. A launch delay can shift a mission into a period with longer darkness or communication gaps. The app helps mission teams see what changes, identify which requirements are affected, and explore alternatives. Its visual tools also help educators and the public understand why lunar terrain and timing matter.

What a four-day delay changes

Our reproducible example is a hypothetical 14-day mission evaluated using NASA-derived data.

  • Original plan: Landing at Peak Near Shackleton on 10 October 2027 at 00:00 UTC meets the selected requirements. The longest Earth-contact gap is 22 hours.
  • Four-day delay: Landing at the same site on 14 October 2027 at 00:00 UTC, with the same duration and requirements, produces a different result. Earth remains visible for 64.9% of the mission, above the 40% minimum. However, one continuous gap lasts 118 hours within the mission, exceeding the 96-hour limit.
  • Recovery: Landing at Malapert Massif on the delayed date meets the unchanged requirements, with no modeled loss of geometric Earth line of sight during the 14-day mission. Changing the landing location by about 143 km would still require a review of science objectives and landing safety.

The failed interval runs from 23 October at 02:00 UTC to the mission boundary on 28 October at 00:00 UTC. The 118 hours describe exposure within the evaluated mission. The physical outage may continue afterward.

Users can follow the failed requirement to its interval and open the relevant site and time in 3D. This example shows why we check continuous gaps alongside mission averages: the overall visibility percentage passes, but the uninterrupted loss of Earth contact breaks the requirement.

How it works

NASA data and terrain geometry. JPL Horizons supplies Sun and Earth directions. LRO LOLA elevation data from NASA Moon Trek defines the terrain skyline around each site. Our model accounts for lunar curvature, samples 720 horizon directions, and calculates how much of the solar disk remains visible above the terrain. The default observer height is 2 m.

The curated library contains 24 sites with hourly data from 1 January 2026 to 1 January 2031. Custom-site calculations use Skyfield with JPL ephemeris and lunar-frame kernels.

One assessment across the planning tools. The deterministic engine checks solar availability, continuous time below the selected solar-visibility threshold, Earth visibility, communication blackouts, and initial operating windows after landing. It returns PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN, together with measurements, margins, and supporting evidence.

Missing data produces bounded ranges. When the available evidence cannot settle a requirement, its result remains UNKNOWN. Only comparable PASS plans receive a rank, and changing preferences cannot override a failed requirement. Scores describe relative desirability under the selected weights, not a probability of mission success.

A shared time policy. Landing time rounds to the nearest UTC hour and mission duration to whole hours. The app shows the requested and evaluated intervals when they differ.

A recorded benchmark of 200 assessments using prepared Malapert data measured a median assessment time of 3.35 ms. This was a single-machine benchmark that excluded data loading and interface latency.

Exploring a plan and finding alternatives

The 3D Mission Planner lets users choose a curated site or enter custom lunar coordinates, adjust dates and mission duration, and inspect conditions over time. A 2D map, 3D terrain view, sky plot, and visibility timeline show different aspects of the same site and time.

Plan comparison shows the decision and the requirements that determine it, with technical detail available for closer inspection. Mission Rescue searches supported sites and sampled dates after a delay or requirement change, then checks alternatives against the same requirements.

The Feasibility Atlas maps landing date against mission duration for one site and spacecraft configuration. Selecting a cell lets users open that evaluated mission in the Planner.

A Mission Report captures the assessed inputs, verdicts, evidence, dataset hashes, and model versions in a frozen snapshot. Users can download it as PDF or JSON. Comparison results also export as CSV and JSON.

The guided tour, available through “Take the guided tour,” introduces newcomers to the original mission, launch delay, failed requirement, 3D evidence, and Rescue recovery. It uses NASA-derived data and results computed by the application. Users seeking more detail can inspect the measurements and methodology directly.

Rover is an optional, read-only AI assistant. It explains computed results in plain language and helps users navigate Plan comparison and its reports. AI answers require a configured backend. When that service is unavailable, the interface labels its basic fallback answers as non-AI.

Scientific checks and limits

A recorded cross-check compared Horizons positions with independent Skyfield/JPL DE421 calculations at 24 sites, sampled every six hours across the stored data range. The maximum angular separation was 0.00072 degrees. This measures agreement between calculations, not observational accuracy or NASA certification.

Separate checks compare horizon methods and modeled illumination with LROC observations. The validation view reports the scope of these checks and where the results disagree.

The prototype provides early screening of illumination and geometric Earth line of sight. A passing result does not establish a complete electrical or radio-link budget, ground-station availability, thermal survival, or landing safety. Hourly sampling can miss short events, and terrain resolution affects results near shadow boundaries.

Technology and intended impact

The frontend uses TypeScript, React, Three.js with React Three Fiber/Drei, OpenLayers, Recharts, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, and Vite. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, NumPy, Rasterio, Astroquery/Astropy, and Skyfield. React-pdf produces Mission Reports. Pytest, Vitest, and Playwright support verification.

For mission teams, our aim is to make site and schedule comparisons easier to review using shared requirements and visible evidence. For educators and the public, the app shows how terrain, and timing and positions of the Sun and the Earth affect lunar exploration.

Our next steps are to test the workflow with mission planners, use finer sampling near requirement boundaries, and extend the electrical and radio modeling.

AI-assisted development

We used SI-assisted tools, including Claude Code and ChatGPT, for slight coding assistance, debugging, documentation, and miscelleaneous queries throughout the Challenge. Rover’s backend includes an OpenRouter integration for optional LLM explanations. The deterministic engine computes scientific measurements, verdicts, scores, and rankings using the cited data sources.
